entries.meaning: To go faster, or to make something go faster. ---
examples: This car accelerates from zero to sixty in six seconds.
She accelerated to pass the truck.
He was accelerating when a deer stepped onto the road.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (accelerate the car), intransitive (the train accelerated)

entries.meaning: To go somewhere together with someone. ---
examples: A guide accompanies every group into the canyon.
Her brother accompanied her to the airport.
Children under twelve must be accompanied by an adult.
entries.transitivity: transitive
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y changes: accompany → accompanies, accompanied, but accompanying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: To move forward, especially steadily or with effort. ---
examples: The line advances about one person a minute.
The troops advanced under cover of darkness.
Storm clouds were advancing from the west.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (advance the ball), intransitive (the line advanced)

entries.meaning: To reach the place you were traveling to. ---
examples: Our flight arrives at six in the morning.
We arrived in Denver two hours late.
The package still has not arrived.
entries.transitivity: intransitive
entries.contrast: arrive in a city or country, arrive at a building or a point. Never arrive to.

entries.meaning: To go up to a higher place. ---
examples: The trail ascends steeply for the first mile.
The balloon ascended until it disappeared.
We spent the morning ascending the ridge.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (ascend the stairs), intransitive (the balloon ascended)

entries.meaning: To get on a plane, train, ship, or bus. ---
examples: Passengers in group C may now board.
We boarded the ferry just before it pulled away.
They have already boarded the plane.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (board the train), intransitive (we boarded at gate 12)

entries.meaning: To spring back after hitting a surface, or to make something do that. ---
examples: He bounces the ball while he thinks.
The ball bounced twice and rolled into the street.
The kids have been bouncing on the bed all morning.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (bounce a ball), intransitive (the ball bounced)

entries.meaning: To slow down or stop a vehicle by using the brakes. ---
examples: He brakes too late on wet roads.
She braked hard when the light turned red.
The truck was braking all the way down the hill.
entries.transitivity: intransitive
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like break (сломать). The silent -e drops before -ing: braking.

entries.meaning: To hold something and move it from one place to another. ---
examples: Let me carry that bag for you.
She carried the sleeping child upstairs.
He was carrying two suitcases and a cup of coffee.
entries.transitivity: transitive
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y changes: carry → carries, carried, but carrying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: To run after someone or something in order to catch them. ---
examples: The dog chases every squirrel in the yard.
Police chased the car for three miles.
She spent the afternoon chasing a toddler around the park.
entries.transitivity: transitive

entries.meaning: To move all the way around something. ---
examples: Hawks circle above that field every evening.
The plane circled the airport for twenty minutes.
We kept circling the block looking for parking.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (circle the airport), intransitive (hawks circled overhead)

entries.meaning: To hit something violently while moving. ---
examples: Meteors collide with the atmosphere and burn up.
Two cars collided at the intersection this morning.
The bus had collided with a guardrail before it stopped.
entries.transitivity: intransitive
entries.contrast: collide with something.

entries.meaning: To travel regularly between your home and your job. ---
examples: I commute forty minutes each way.
She commuted into the city for eleven years.
He has been commuting by train since March.
entries.русский: ездить на работу и обратно, добираться
entries.transitivity: intransitive

entries.meaning: To keep going without stopping. ---
examples: Continue straight for two miles, then turn right.
The road continued past the last farmhouse.
The rain has continued all night.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (continue the trip), intransitive (the road continues)

entries.meaning: To hit something hard and be damaged, especially in a vehicle. ---
examples: Planes rarely crash, but people still worry.
He crashed his bike into a mailbox.
A truck had crashed on the on-ramp, so we sat there for an hour.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (crash the car), intransitive (the plane crashed)
entries.contrast: crash into something. Third person adds -es: crashes.

entries.meaning: To move forward on your hands and knees, or to move very slowly. ---
examples: The baby crawls everywhere now.
We crawled under the fence.
Traffic was crawling along at five miles an hour.
entries.transitivity: intransitive

entries.meaning: To go from one side of something to the other. ---
examples: Look both ways before you cross.
We crossed the border a little after noon.
They have crossed that river three times today.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (cross the street), intransitive (cross at the light)
entries.contrast: Third person adds -es after -ss: crosses.

entries.meaning: To travel smoothly at a steady speed, especially by ship or car. ---
examples: The plane cruises at thirty-five thousand feet.
We cruised down the coast with the windows open.
They spent a week cruising the Caribbean.
entries.русский: путешествовать на теплоходе; ехать не спеша
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (cruise the coast), intransitive (the plane cruises)

entries.meaning: To run somewhere very quickly and for a short distance. ---
examples: He dashes out for coffee every morning at ten.
She dashed across the platform and caught the train.
I was dashing to the gate when they called my name.
entries.transitivity: intransitive

entries.meaning: To take goods or mail to the place where they were sent. ---
examples: They deliver between nine and noon.
The driver delivered the package to the wrong door.
We are delivering the furniture on Thursday.
entries.transitivity: transitive
entries.contrast: Stress is on the middle syllable, so the r is not doubled: delivered, delivering.

entries.meaning: To leave, especially on a scheduled trip. ---
examples: The last bus departs at eleven forty.
We departed an hour behind schedule.
The ship was departing as we ran down the dock.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (depart the station), intransitive (the train departed)
entries.contrast: depart from a place. It is the formal opposite of arrive.

entries.meaning: To move down to a lower place. ---
examples: The plane began to descend over the lake.
We descended the stairs in the dark.
Fog was descending on the whole valley.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (descend the stairs), intransitive (the plane descended)

entries.meaning: To bring a boat to a dock, or to arrive at one. ---
examples: The ferry docks every hour on the hour.
Our ship docked in Miami at dawn.
They were still docking when the storm hit.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (dock the boat), intransitive (the ferry docked)

entries.meaning: To pull something heavy along the ground. ---
examples: Do not drag the couch across the floor.
He dragged the trash cans out to the curb.
She was dragging a suitcase with a broken wheel.
entries.transitivity: transitive
entries.contrast: One vowel + one consonant, so the g doubles: dragged, dragging.

entries.meaning: To be carried slowly along by water, air, or a current. ---
examples: We let the canoe drift for a while.
The raft drifted two miles downstream overnight.
Leaves were drifting across the empty road.
entries.transitivity: intransitive

entries.meaning: To let something fall, or to fall suddenly. ---
examples: Be careful not to drop the eggs.
She dropped her keys through the grate.
The temperature has dropped twenty degrees since noon.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (drop the keys), intransitive (the temperature dropped)
entries.contrast: One vowel + one consonant, so the p doubles: dropped, dropping.

entries.meaning: To get on a ship or plane, or to start a journey. ---
examples: Passengers embark at the south terminal.
We embarked in Seattle on a rainy morning.
They are embarking on a year-long trip around Asia.
entries.русский: садиться на судно; отправляться в путь
entries.transitivity: intransitive
entries.contrast: embark on a journey or a project.

entries.meaning: To go with someone in order to guide or protect them. ---
examples: A guard will escort you to the exit.
Two police cars escorted the convoy.
She was escorted through the crowd by security.
entries.transitivity: transitive
entries.contrast: The verb is stressed on the second syllable, i-SKORT; the noun is ES-kort.

entries.meaning: To get away from someone who is chasing or looking for you. ---
examples: Deer evade hunters by moving at night.
The suspect evaded police for six days.
He has evaded capture twice already.
entries.transitivity: transitive

entries.meaning: To go out of a place, or to leave a highway. ---
examples: Exit at the next ramp and turn left.
We exited the theater through a side door.
Cars were exiting onto the service road.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (exit the building), intransitive (exit at the next ramp)
entries.contrast: Stress is on the first syllable, so the t is not doubled: exited, exiting.

entries.meaning: To travel through an unfamiliar place in order to learn about it. ---
examples: Let us explore the old part of town.
They explored the caves with headlamps.
We spent Saturday exploring the coast road.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (explore the caves), intransitive (we explored on foot)

entries.meaning: To carry people or goods across water or over a short distance. ---
examples: A small boat ferries hikers to the island.
His dad ferried us to practice every Tuesday.
Helicopters were ferrying supplies to the flooded town.
entries.transitivity: transitive
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y changes: ferry → ferries, ferried, but ferrying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: To stay on the surface of a liquid, or to move gently through the air. ---
examples: Wood floats, stone does not.
The raft floated downstream all afternoon.
Balloons were floating over the parking lot.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (float a log downstream), intransitive (wood floats)

entries.meaning: To move steadily and continuously, the way a liquid does. ---
examples: The river flows south into the bay.
Traffic flowed smoothly once the extra lane opened.
Water was flowing across the road.
entries.transitivity: intransitive

entries.meaning: To go after or behind someone or something. ---
examples: Follow me, I know a shortcut.
A gray car followed us for a few blocks.
The dog has been following him around all day.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (follow me), intransitive (you go first, I will follow)

entries.meaning: To move smoothly and quietly without visible effort. ---
examples: Skaters glide across that pond all winter.
The canoe glided under the bridge.
A hawk was gliding on the warm air above the field.
entries.transitivity: intransitive

entries.meaning: To show someone the way by going with them. ---
examples: A ranger will guide you to the falls.
She guided us through the market.
He has been guiding rafting trips for ten years.
entries.transitivity: transitive

entries.meaning: To stop moving, or to make something stop. ---
examples: Snow halts traffic on this pass every year.
The convoy halted at the checkpoint.
Work has been halted until the inspection is done.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (halt the traffic), intransitive (the convoy halted)

entries.meaning: To pull or carry something heavy over a distance. ---
examples: That truck can haul four tons.
We hauled the canoe up the bank.
He was hauling firewood all morning.
entries.transitivity: transitive

entries.meaning: To go in a particular direction. ---
examples: We head out at six tomorrow.
She headed straight for the exit.
Storm clouds were heading our way.
entries.transitivity: intransitive
entries.contrast: head for or head toward a place.

entries.meaning: To take a long walk in the country or the mountains. ---
examples: We hike that ridge every fall.
They hiked eleven miles in one day.
She has been hiking since she was a kid.
entries.русский: ходить в поход, идти пешком (по горам, лесу)
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (hike the ridge), intransitive (we hiked all day)

entries.meaning: To jump on one foot or in short light jumps, or to get quickly on or off something. ---
examples: Hop in, I will drive you.
The rabbit hopped across the yard.
He was hopping on one foot after the game.
entries.transitivity: intransitive
entries.contrast: One vowel + one consonant, so the p doubles: hopped, hopping. Compare hope → hoped, hoping.

entries.meaning: To stay in one place in the air. ---
examples: Hummingbirds hover while they feed.
A helicopter hovered over the freeway.
The drone was hovering just above the roof.
entries.transitivity: intransitive

entries.meaning: To move or do something more quickly than usual. ---
examples: Hurry or we will miss the train.
She hurried down the platform.
They were hurrying to finish before the rain.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (hurry the kids along), intransitive (we hurried)
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y changes: hurry → hurries, hurried, but hurrying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: To run slowly and steadily for exercise. ---
examples: I jog three mornings a week.
He jogged around the reservoir.
She was jogging when the storm started.
entries.transitivity: intransitive
entries.contrast: One vowel + one consonant, so the g doubles: jogged, jogging.

entries.meaning: To push yourself off the ground with your legs. ---
examples: Do not jump off that wall.
He jumped over the puddle.
The kids have been jumping in the leaves.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (jump the fence), intransitive (he jumped)

entries.meaning: To come down onto the ground after being in the air. ---
examples: The plane lands at four fifteen.
We landed in Chicago in a snowstorm.
A bird was landing on the wire outside.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (land the plane), intransitive (we landed on time)

entries.meaning: To send something into the air or the water, or to start it moving. ---
examples: They launch the boat from the ramp.
NASA launched the rocket at dawn.
Crews were launching rescue boats all night.
entries.transitivity: transitive
entries.contrast: Third person adds -es after -ch: launches.

entries.meaning: To raise something to a higher position. ---
examples: Can you lift the other end?
He lifted the bike onto the rack.
She was lifting boxes into the truck all morning.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (lift the box), intransitive (the fog lifted)

entries.meaning: To walk with difficulty because one leg hurts. ---
examples: She still limps a little in cold weather.
He limped off the field.
The dog was limping after the long walk.
entries.transitivity: intransitive

entries.meaning: To put things into or onto a vehicle or a container. ---
examples: Help me load the car.
They loaded the truck in twenty minutes.
We were still loading when the movers arrived.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (load the truck), intransitive (we loaded up and left)

entries.meaning: To send something through the postal system. ---
examples: I will mail the forms tomorrow.
She mailed the package on Friday.
They have already mailed the tickets.
entries.transitivity: transitive
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like male.

entries.meaning: To walk with regular steps, especially as part of a group. ---
examples: The band marches onto the field at halftime.
Thousands marched down the avenue.
Soldiers were marching past the gate.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (march the prisoners out), intransitive (the band marched)
entries.contrast: Third person adds -es after -ch: marches.

entries.meaning: To join a line of moving traffic, or to combine into one. ---
examples: Merge carefully, that lane ends soon.
He merged onto the highway without signaling.
Two lanes were merging into one.
entries.русский: вливаться, влиться; перестраиваться в общий поток
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (merge the two lanes), intransitive (merge onto the highway)
entries.contrast: merge onto a highway, merge with something.

entries.meaning: To move from one region to another, usually with the seasons. ---
examples: Geese migrate south every fall.
His family migrated west during the Depression.
Whales are migrating along the coast right now.
entries.transitivity: intransitive

entries.meaning: To change place or position, or to go and live somewhere else. ---
examples: Please move your car.
They moved to Portland last spring.
The line has not moved in ten minutes.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (move the car), intransitive (the line moved)

entries.meaning: To find the way when traveling, or to steer a ship or plane. ---
examples: You drive and I will navigate.
They navigated by the stars.
She was navigating from a paper map.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (navigate the channel), intransitive (you drive, I will navigate)

entries.meaning: To walk back and forth in the same small space. ---
examples: She paces whenever she is on the phone.
He paced the hallway outside the room.
They were pacing the waiting room for hours.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (pace the hallway), intransitive (he paced nervously)

entries.meaning: To put your things into a bag or a box before a trip. ---
examples: I still have to pack.
She packed two sweaters and a raincoat.
He was packing at midnight the night before the flight.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (pack a bag), intransitive (I still have to pack)

entries.meaning: To move a small boat through water with a paddle. ---
examples: They paddle the same river every summer.
We paddled across the lake before sunrise.
He was paddling hard against the current.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (paddle a canoe), intransitive (we paddled upstream)

entries.meaning: To leave a vehicle somewhere for a period of time. ---
examples: You cannot park here on Tuesdays.
She parked two blocks away.
We have been parking in the garage all week.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (park the car), intransitive (park in the back)

entries.meaning: To go by someone or something, or to move past it. ---
examples: We pass the lake on the way home.
A truck passed us on the right.
They were passing through Ohio when the call came.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (pass the truck), intransitive (a car passed on the right)
entries.contrast: Third person adds -es: passes. The past form passed sounds exactly like past.

entries.meaning: To stop for a short time before going on. ---
examples: He pauses before every answer.
She paused at the top of the stairs.
They were pausing every few minutes to rest.
entries.русский: делать паузу, приостанавливаться, остановиться на миг
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (pause the video), intransitive (she paused at the door)

entries.meaning: To push the pedals of a bicycle to make it move. ---
examples: Pedal faster up this part.
He pedaled the last mile standing up.
She was pedaling into a headwind.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (pedal a bike), intransitive (he pedaled uphill)
entries.contrast: American spelling keeps one l: pedaled, pedaling (British pedalled, pedalling). Do not confuse with peddle (торговать вразнос).

entries.meaning: To go on to the next place or the next step. ---
examples: Please proceed to gate fourteen.
We proceeded down the hall as instructed.
The parade was proceeding slowly up Main Street.
entries.transitivity: intransitive
entries.contrast: Double -ee-: proceed, not procede. Different from precede (предшествовать).

entries.meaning: To move something toward you by taking hold of it. ---
examples: Pull the door, do not push it.
He pulled the sled up the hill.
She was pulling a wagon full of kids.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (pull the door), intransitive (pull harder)

entries.meaning: To follow someone in order to catch or reach them. ---
examples: Wolves pursue a herd for miles.
Two patrol cars pursued the van across town.
Officers were pursuing the suspect on foot.
entries.transitivity: transitive

entries.meaning: To move something away from you by pressing on it. ---
examples: Push the cart over here.
He pushed the stalled car off the road.
She was pushing a stroller up the hill.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (push the cart), intransitive (push harder)
entries.contrast: Third person adds -es after -sh: pushes.

entries.meaning: To move very fast, or to compete for speed. ---
examples: Do not race down the stairs.
He raced to the gate and just made it.
They were racing each other to the mailbox.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (race him to the corner), intransitive (he raced home)

entries.meaning: To move to a different place to live or work. ---
examples: The company wants to relocate him to Austin.
They relocated to Arizona after he retired.
We are relocating the office next month.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (relocate the office), intransitive (they relocated to Arizona)

entries.meaning: To stay in the same place instead of leaving. ---
examples: Please remain seated until we reach the gate.
She remained on the platform until the train was out of sight.
Only three passengers have remained on board.
entries.transitivity: intransitive

entries.meaning: To take something away from a place. ---
examples: Please remove your bags from the aisle.
They removed the roadblock at noon.
Snow has been removed from the main roads.
entries.transitivity: transitive

entries.meaning: To move back away from a difficult or dangerous place. ---
examples: Glaciers retreat a little further every year.
The army retreated across the river.
We were retreating to the car as the rain started.
entries.transitivity: intransitive

entries.meaning: To come or go back to a place, or to give something back. ---
examples: They return from Spain on Sunday.
He returned to the same hotel every summer.
She has not returned my call.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (return the keys), intransitive (they returned late)

entries.meaning: To drive backward, or to turn something the opposite way. ---
examples: Reverse slowly, the driveway is narrow.
He reversed into a parking space.
The truck was reversing when it hit the pole.
entries.русский: ехать задним ходом, сдавать назад; менять на противоположное
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (reverse the car), intransitive (he reversed slowly)

entries.meaning: To move around a wide area without a fixed direction. ---
examples: Cattle roam the whole valley.
We roamed the old city for hours.
A stray dog had been roaming the neighborhood for weeks.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (roam the hills), intransitive (cattle roam free)

entries.meaning: To move by turning over and over, or to make something do that. ---
examples: Waves roll in all afternoon.
The ball rolled under the car.
He was rolling the barrel toward the truck.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (roll the barrel), intransitive (the ball rolled)
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like role (роль).

entries.meaning: To turn around a center point. ---
examples: The Earth rotates once a day.
He rotated the tires before the trip.
The beam was rotating slowly above the harbor.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (rotate the tires), intransitive (the Earth rotates)

entries.meaning: To move a boat through water using oars. ---
examples: They row on the river every morning.
We rowed out to the island.
She was rowing against a strong wind.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (row the boat), intransitive (they row every morning)
entries.contrast: The verb is /roʊ/, rhyming with go — not the noun row /raʊ/ that means ссора.

entries.meaning: To go somewhere or do something very quickly. ---
examples: Do not rush, we have time.
They rushed him to the hospital.
Everyone was rushing for the last train.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (rush him to the hospital), intransitive (do not rush)

entries.meaning: To travel on water in a boat or a ship. ---
examples: We sail at first light.
The ferry sailed without us.
They have been sailing the coast all summer.
entries.русский: плыть на судне, идти под парусом; отплывать
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (sail the coast), intransitive (we sail at dawn)
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like sale (распродажа).

entries.meaning: To move apart quickly in different directions, or to throw things around. ---
examples: Wind scatters the leaves across the yard.
The birds scattered when the door slammed.
People were scattering in every direction.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (scatter the seed), intransitive (the birds scattered)

entries.meaning: To move something a short distance, or to change position. ---
examples: Can you shift the couch a little to the left?
The wind shifted to the north overnight.
He kept shifting the box from arm to arm.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (shift the couch), intransitive (the wind shifted)

entries.meaning: To send goods somewhere by truck, ship, or plane. ---
examples: We ship anywhere in the country.
They shipped the order on Monday.
Your package is shipping today.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (ship the order), intransitive (we ship on Mondays)
entries.contrast: One vowel + one consonant, so the p doubles: shipped, shipping.

entries.meaning: To travel back and forth between two places, or to carry people that way. ---
examples: A van shuttles guests to the airport.
He shuttled between two offices for years.
Buses were shuttling fans from the lot to the stadium.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (shuttle guests to the airport), intransitive (he shuttled between two offices)

entries.meaning: To show which way you are turning, or to give someone a sign. ---
examples: Always signal before you change lanes.
She signaled left and slowed down.
The officer was signaling us to pull over.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (signal a turn), intransitive (signal before you merge)
entries.contrast: American spelling keeps one l: signaled, signaling (British signalled, signalling).

entries.meaning: To slide sideways on a road after losing grip. ---
examples: Bald tires skid in the rain.
The car skidded on black ice.
The truck was skidding toward the guardrail.
entries.transitivity: intransitive
entries.contrast: One vowel + one consonant, so the d doubles: skidded, skidding.

entries.meaning: To move along with light hops from one foot to the other. ---
examples: Kids skip when they are happy.
She skipped down the sidewalk.
He was skipping stones across the water.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (skip a stone), intransitive (she skipped down the street)
entries.contrast: One vowel + one consonant, so the p doubles: skipped, skipping.

entries.meaning: To slide by accident and lose your balance, or to move quietly. ---
examples: Be careful, you could slip.
He slipped on the wet steps.
She was slipping out the back door when we saw her.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (slip the note under the door), intransitive (he slipped on the ice)
entries.contrast: One vowel + one consonant, so the p doubles: slipped, slipping.

entries.meaning: To fly high in the air without much effort. ---
examples: Eagles soar over the canyon.
The kite soared above the beach.
Gulls were soaring on the wind off the water.
entries.transitivity: intransitive
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like sore (больной, воспалённый).

entries.meaning: To run as fast as you can for a short distance. ---
examples: She sprints the last hundred meters.
He sprinted for the closing doors.
I was sprinting across the terminal with two bags.
entries.transitivity: intransitive

entries.meaning: To follow a person or an animal quietly in order to catch or watch them. ---
examples: Lions stalk their prey for hours.
The cat stalked a bird across the lawn.
He had been stalking the herd since dawn.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (stalk the deer), intransitive (the cat stalked closer)
entries.contrast: The l is silent: STAWK.

entries.meaning: To remain in a place instead of leaving. ---
examples: Stay here while I get the car.
We stayed in a motel outside town.
They have been staying with friends since the flood.
entries.transitivity: intransitive
entries.contrast: Vowel + -y keeps the y: stayed, never staid.

entries.meaning: To control the direction of a vehicle or a boat. ---
examples: This boat steers better with two people aboard.
He steered with one hand.
She was steering while he read the map.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (steer the boat), intransitive (he steers with one hand)

entries.meaning: To move by putting one foot down in a new place. ---
examples: Step back from the platform edge.
She stepped over the puddle.
He was stepping off the curb when the bike went by.
entries.transitivity: intransitive
entries.contrast: One vowel + one consonant, so the p doubles: stepped, stepping.

entries.meaning: To end movement, or to make something end. ---
examples: The bus stops at every corner.
We stopped for gas outside Barstow.
It has not stopped raining since Tuesday.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (stop the car), intransitive (the bus stopped)
entries.contrast: One vowel + one consonant, so the p doubles: stopped, stopping. Compare hope → hoped, hoping.

entries.meaning: To wander away from the right place or path. ---
examples: Do not stray from the trail.
The dog strayed into the neighbor's yard.
A few sheep had strayed onto the road.
entries.transitivity: intransitive

entries.meaning: To walk slowly and in a relaxed way. ---
examples: They stroll through the park after dinner.
We strolled along the waterfront.
An old couple was strolling ahead of us.
entries.transitivity: intransitive

entries.meaning: To hit your foot on something and almost fall. ---
examples: People stumble on that step all the time.
He stumbled on a loose brick.
She was stumbling in the dark without a flashlight.
entries.transitivity: intransitive

entries.meaning: To be or move all around something on every side. ---
examples: Mountains surround the town.
Police surrounded the building.
The house is surrounded by tall pines.
entries.transitivity: transitive

entries.meaning: To turn suddenly to one side while moving. ---
examples: The bus swerves around that pothole every day.
He swerved to miss a deer.
A car was swerving between lanes ahead of us.
entries.transitivity: intransitive

entries.meaning: To walk quietly on the front part of your feet. ---
examples: Tiptoe past the baby's room.
She tiptoed down the hall.
He was tiptoeing around the squeaky boards.
entries.transitivity: intransitive
entries.contrast: The e stays before -ing: tiptoeing.

entries.meaning: To travel around a place, visiting the interesting parts. ---
examples: The band tours every summer.
We toured the old mission in the morning.
They are touring the national parks in a camper.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (tour the museum), intransitive (the band tours in July)

entries.meaning: To pull a vehicle or a boat behind another one. ---
examples: They will tow your car if you park here.
A pickup towed us to the shop.
His truck was towing a boat up the grade.
entries.transitivity: transitive
entries.contrast: /toʊ/ rhymes with go and sounds exactly like toe.

entries.meaning: To follow the marks or signals that show where someone or something has gone. ---
examples: You can track the package online.
Rangers tracked the bear for two days.
We were tracking the storm all evening.
entries.transitivity: transitive

entries.meaning: To follow slowly behind someone, or to hang down and drag along. ---
examples: The youngest kid always trails the group.
Two reporters trailed the bus all day.
Her scarf was trailing in the snow.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (trail the suspect), intransitive (the youngest kid trailed behind)

entries.meaning: To move from one place, vehicle, or line to another. ---
examples: You transfer at Union Station.
They transferred him to a hospital in the city.
We were transferring to another flight when the storm hit.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (transfer the patient), intransitive (transfer at Union Station)
entries.contrast: Stress falls on the last syllable, so the r doubles: transferred, transferring.

entries.meaning: To carry people or goods from one place to another. ---
examples: Trucks transport most of the grain.
The injured were transported by helicopter.
They are transporting the sculpture in three pieces.
entries.transitivity: transitive
entries.contrast: The verb is stressed on the second syllable, trans-PORT; the noun is TRANS-port.

entries.meaning: To go from one place to another, especially over a long distance. ---
examples: They travel for work about once a month.
We traveled through five states in a week.
She has been traveling since Tuesday.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (travel the country), intransitive (they travel for work)
entries.contrast: American spelling keeps one l: traveled, traveling, traveler (British travelled, travelling, traveller).

entries.meaning: To catch your foot on something and lose your balance. ---
examples: Watch out or you will trip.
He tripped over the doorframe.
She was tripping on the hem of her coat all evening.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (trip the runner), intransitive (he tripped on the step)
entries.contrast: One vowel + one consonant, so the p doubles: tripped, tripping. Usually trip over something.

entries.meaning: To fall or roll over suddenly and helplessly. ---
examples: Kids tumble down that hill all summer.
A rock tumbled down the slope.
Bags were tumbling off the cart.
entries.transitivity: intransitive

entries.meaning: To change direction, or to move something around a point. ---
examples: Turn left at the second light.
She turned the corner and disappeared.
The car ahead was turning without signaling.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (turn the wheel), intransitive (turn at the light)

entries.meaning: To bend or curve in a changing direction, or to turn something with your hand. ---
examples: The road twists through the hills.
He twisted his ankle on the trail.
The path was twisting back on itself.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (twist the cap), intransitive (the road twists)

entries.meaning: To take things off a vehicle or out of a container. ---
examples: Help me unload the van.
They unloaded the truck in the rain.
We were still unloading at midnight.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (unload the van), intransitive (we unloaded in the rain)

entries.meaning: To take things out of a bag or a box after a trip. ---
examples: I have not had time to unpack.
She unpacked as soon as we got in.
He was unpacking when the phone rang.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (unpack the suitcase), intransitive (I have not unpacked yet)

entries.meaning: To change direction suddenly, especially while moving. ---
examples: The trail veers right after the bridge.
The truck veered onto the shoulder.
A car was veering toward us.
entries.transitivity: intransitive

entries.meaning: To go to see a person or a place and spend some time there. ---
examples: We visit her parents every Thanksgiving.
They visited three cities in five days.
He has visited the museum twice this month.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (visit her parents), intransitive (they are just visiting)
entries.contrast: Stress is on the first syllable, so the t is not doubled: visited, visiting.

entries.meaning: To walk through water that is not deep. ---
examples: Herons wade along the shallow edge.
We waded across the creek.
She was wading out to the sandbar.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (wade the creek), intransitive (we waded ashore)

entries.meaning: To move on foot at a normal speed. ---
examples: I walk to work when it is dry.
We walked the last half mile.
He has been walking for two hours.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (walk the dog), intransitive (I walk to work)
entries.contrast: The l is silent: WAWK.

entries.meaning: To walk around slowly with no particular destination. ---
examples: He wanders off whenever we stop.
We wandered through the market all morning.
Tourists were wandering around the square.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (wander the streets), intransitive (he wandered off)
entries.contrast: wander /ˈwɑːndər/ (бродить) is not wonder /ˈwʌndər/ (удивляться, задаваться вопросом).

entries.meaning: To let other traffic go first.
examples: Yield to cars already in the circle.
He yielded to the truck coming down the ramp.
Drivers were not yielding at the crosswalk.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (yield the right of way), intransitive (yield to traffic in the circle)
